# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Q1. `[KTU University Exam - May 2024 Set A]`
**Explain the function of the shoulder in an FSW tool. Why is the shoulder diameter typically chosen as 3× the pin diameter?**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

The shoulder in an FSW tool serves three primary functions:
1. **Heat generation** — through frictional contact with the workpiece top surface. It contributes approximately **80–85%** of the total heat input, with the remaining 15–20% coming from the pin.
2. **Forging pressure** — applies the downward axial force that consolidates the material behind the pin and prevents tunnel defects.
3. **Containment** — confines the plasticized metal beneath it, preventing flash and supporting the formation of a sound stir zone.

**Why 3× ratio:**
- Ensures a *heat-affected zone* wide enough to soften the surrounding material uniformly.
- Provides sufficient *plasticized material reservoir* to replenish the trailing side.
- Prevents *excess flash* (which would occur if shoulder were >4×) and *insufficient forging* (which would occur if <2×).
- Recommended by **Mishra & Ma (2005)** as the empirical optimum for aluminium alloys. **(1 mark for ratio justification)**

### Q2. `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023 Set B]`
**Differentiate between the advancing side and the retreating side in FSW. What defect is most likely on the advancing side and why?**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| Feature | Advancing Side (AS) | Retreating Side (RS) |
|---|---|---|
| Velocity relation | Tool rotation tangent velocity **aligned** with welding direction | Tool rotation tangent velocity **opposite** to welding direction |
| Material behavior | Material is **dragged forward** with the tool | Material is **swept backward** |
| Material supply | Often **deficient** | Often **excess** |
| Defect type | **Tunnel voids** (longitudinal cavities) | **Flash** (excess material) and surface galling |

**Defect on AS — Tunnel void (1 mark for explanation):**
On the AS, the tool removes material as it advances, but insufficient plasticized metal flows in to refill the void. This creates a continuous tunnel-like cavity along the weld line, particularly when the tool is too cold, the pin is too short, or the welding speed is too high for the chosen rotational speed.

## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each) — Module Internal Choice

### Question A (14 Marks) — `[KTU ESE - Module 2 Choice Option A]`

**(a)** With the help of a neat sketch, describe the various pin profiles used in FSW tools. Explain the effect of **threaded pin profile** on the direction of material flow. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Derive the expression for the total heat input rate during FSW, including both shoulder and pin contributions. A 6 mm thick Al 6082 plate is welded at $N = 1000$ RPM, $v = 80$ mm/min, with shoulder force $F_{sh} = 10$ kN, shoulder radius $R_{sh} = 9$ mm, pin radius $R_p = 3$ mm, pin force $F_p = 2$ kN, and $\mu = 0.45$. Calculate the **spindle power** and the **heat input per unit length** of weld, assuming heat efficiency $\eta = 0.85$. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution

**(a) Pin Profiles and Threaded Pin Effect (7 marks):**

Pin profiles (1 mark for sketch, 1 mark per profile × 4 = 4 marks, 2 marks for threaded-pin flow effect):

1. **Cylindrical / Straight pin** — constant cross-section, simplest design. Good for thin sheets; limited vertical flow.
2. **Tapered / Conical pin** — diameter reduces from top to bottom; provides strong downward and lateral flow; ideal for thick plates.
3. **Threaded pin** — helical ridges act as an *auger*. **Right-hand threads with clockwise rotation** drive material *downward* (most common). **Left-hand threads with clockwise rotation** drive material *upward* (used to avoid flash on exit side).
4. **Fluted / Triflate pin** — three or four flat surfaces act as additional shear planes; increases surface area, torque, and material mixing.

**Sketch (descriptive):** A vertical cross-section of a tool showing shoulder (D_sh) at top and pin (d_p) below with various profiles annotated. *(1 mark)*

**Threaded Pin and Flow (2 marks):** A right-hand threaded pin when rotated clockwise acts as a screw pump, generating an *axial downward material flow* along with the rotational tangential flow. This downward component is critical for:
- Refilling the advancing side to prevent tunnel defects.
- Forging the retreating side material into the weld line.
- Improving the consolidation of onion-ring features.

---

**(b) Heat Input Derivation and Numerical (7 marks):**

**Derivation (4 marks):**
Same as in **Section 3.1** above. Key results:
- $P_{sh} = \dfrac{2 \pi N \mu F_{sh} R_{sh}}{60}$
- $P_p = \dfrac{2 \pi N \mu F_p R_p}{60}$
- $P_{tot} = P_{sh} + P_p$
- $E_{line} = \dfrac{\eta \cdot P_{tot}}{v}$

**Numerical (3 marks):**
Given: $N = 1000$ RPM, $v = 80$ mm/min $= 80/60$ m/s $= 1.333$ m/s, $F_{sh} = 10\,000$ N, $R_{sh} = 0.009$ m, $F_p = 2000$ N, $R_p = 0.003$ m, $\mu = 0.45$, $\eta = 0.85$.

**Step 1 — Power at shoulder.**

$$
P_{sh} = \dfrac{2 \pi \times 1000 \times 0.45 \times 10000 \times 0.009}{60}
$$

$$
P_{sh} = \dfrac{2 \pi \times 40.5}{60} = \dfrac{254.47}{60} \approx 4.241 \ \text{kW}
$$

**Step 2 — Power at pin.**

$$
P_p = \dfrac{2 \pi \times 1000 \times 0.45 \times 2000 \times 0.003}{60}
$$

$$
P_p = \dfrac{2 \pi \times 2.7}{60} = \dfrac{16.96}{60} \approx 0.283 \ \text{kW}
$$

**Step 3 — Total spindle power.**

$$
P_{tot} = 4.241 + 0.283 = 4.524 \ \text{kW}
$$

**Step 4 — Useful heat per unit length.**

$$
Q_{useful} = 0.85 \times 4524 = 3845.4 \ \text{W}
$$

$$
E_{line} = \dfrac{Q_{useful}}{v} = \dfrac{3845.4}{1.333} \approx 2885 \ \text{J/m} = 2.885 \ \text{kJ/m}
$$

**Final Answer:** $P_{tot} \approx 4.52$ kW; $E_{line} \approx 2.89$ kJ/m

### Question B (14 Marks) — `[KTU ESE - Module 2 Choice Option B]`

**(a)** Discuss the **four metal flow zones** around an FSW tool. What are the major flow defects, and how are they related to inadequate flow? **(7 marks)**

**(b)** A non-threaded cylindrical pin FSW tool is used to weld 4 mm AA 6061 plates. The tool has $D_{sh} = 15$ mm, $d_p = 5$ mm, $N = 1200$ RPM, $v = 100$ mm/min, $F_{sh} = 8$ kN, $F_p = 1.5$ kN, $\mu = 0.4$, $\eta = 0.85$. Determine the **total spindle power**, **spindle torque**, and the **effective strain rate** in the stir zone, assuming $L_p = 3.9$ mm. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution

**(a) Four Metal Flow Zones and Flow Defects (7 marks):**

1. **Pre-heat (Leading) Zone** — material ahead of the tool, *not yet deformed*. Heated by conduction from shoulder. (1 mark)
2. **Initial Deformation Zone** — material first contacts the leading edge of the pin. *Heated + plastically deformed*, dragged upward with the tool rotation. (1 mark)
3. **Stir / Extrusion Zone (SZ)** — material undergoes **simple shear** around the pin; forced from AS to RS. The **onion-ring pattern** forms here due to alternating layers of material. (2 marks)
4. **Consolidation / Cooling Zone** — material behind the tool cools under shoulder pressure, *forging the joint*. Coarse recrystallized grains form in this zone. (1 mark)

**Flow Defects (2 marks):**
- **Tunnel void** on AS — insufficient downward/refilling flow.
- **Lazy S / Zigzag line** — incomplete intermixing across weld line.
- **Kissing bond on RS** — inadequate forging pressure on retreating side.
- **Flash on top surface** — over-flow due to excessive tilt or low viscosity.
- **Surface galling** — inadequate shoulder contact.

---

**(b) Numerical (7 marks):**

**Step 1 — Spindle power (3 marks).**

$P_{tot} = \dfrac{2 \pi N \mu}{60}(F_{sh} R_{sh} + F_p R_p)$

$R_{sh} = D_{sh}/2 = 7.5$ mm = 0.0075 m; $R_p = 2.5$ mm = 0.0025 m

$P_{tot} = \dfrac{2 \pi \times 1200 \times 0.4}{60} \times (8000 \times 0.0075 + 1500 \times 0.0025)$

$P_{tot} = \dfrac{2 \pi \times 480}{60} \times (60 + 3.75) = 16 \pi \times 63.75$

$P_{tot} = 50.265 \times 63.75 \approx 3204$ W = 3.20 kW

**Step 2 — Spindle torque (2 marks).**

$T_s = \dfrac{60 \cdot P_{tot}}{2 \pi N} = \dfrac{60 \times 3204}{2 \pi \times 1200}$

$T_s = \dfrac{192240}{7539.8} \approx 25.5$ N·m

**Step 3 — Effective strain rate (2 marks).**

$\dot{\varepsilon} = \dfrac{\pi N r_p}{30 L_p \sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{\pi \times 1200 \times 0.0025}{30 \times 0.0039 \times 1.732}$

$\dot{\varepsilon} = \dfrac{9.425}{0.2026} \approx 46.5$ s⁻¹

**Final Answer:** $P_{tot} \approx 3.20$ kW; $T_s \approx 25.5$ N·m; $\dot{\varepsilon} \approx 46.5$ s⁻¹

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mark-Loss Traps in PEMET416 Module 2 — Tools and Metal Flow:**
> 1. **Mixing up AS/RS:** Students often say "defects form on the retreating side" — WRONG for tunnel voids. The tunnel is on the **advancing side**. The retreating side shows *flash* and *lazy S*. *(–1 mark)*
> 2. **Forgetting units in $E_{line}$:** Heat input per unit length must be in **J/m or kJ/m**. If you write watts (W), you have *forgotten to divide by v*. *(–1 mark)*
> 3. **Wrong pin-thread rule:** "Right-hand thread always pumps material down" is correct ONLY if the tool rotates **clockwise (looking from above)**. State both conditions. *(–1 mark)*
> 4. **Conflating shoulder and pin heat contributions:** Examiner expects you to show $Q_{sh} \approx 80\%$ and $Q_p \approx 20\%$. A single lumped formula without this ratio breakdown loses **0.5–1 mark**.
> 5. **Forgetting efficiency factor $\eta$:** Always state $\eta$ explicitly; otherwise the answer is "idealized".
> 6. **Mermaid diagrams used as physical sketches:** Mermaid is for *flow charts*, not engineering drawings. Draw the pin profile with ASCII art or describe it clearly. *(No negative mark, but 0 for the sketch sub-part.)*
> 7. **Ignoring tool tilt in flow direction:** At a $2°$–$3°$ tilt, the shoulder has a *vertical forging component* $V_{vert} = V_{tan} \sin \theta$ that helps close the AS tunnel. Students often forget this and lose the conceptual mark.

## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> **High-Density Rapid Revision Checklist — Tools and Metal Flow**

- ✅ FSW tool = **Shoulder (heat + forge)** + **Pin (stir + flow)** + **Shank**.
- ✅ Tool is **non-consumable** and works in the **solid state** (no melting).
- ✅ Shoulder generates **~80%** of heat; pin generates **~20%**.
- ✅ Standard shoulder-to-pin diameter ratio = **3 : 1**.
- ✅ Tool tilt = **2°–3°** (typical) to ensure vertical forging and AS refill.
- ✅ Common pin materials: **H13 tool steel, MP159, W–Re, PCBN** (for steel/Ti).
- ✅ **Right-hand threaded pin + clockwise rotation = downward material pumping** (key KTU fact).
- ✅ Flow zones: Pre-heat → Initial Deformation → Stir/Extrusion → Consolidation.
- ✅ **AS (advancing side) → tunnel void**; **RS (retreating side) → flash & kissing bond**.
- ✅ **Onion ring** formation is the *visual signature* of adequate flow.
- ✅ Spindle power formula: $P = \dfrac{2 \pi N T_s}{60}$ — must be **memorized**.
- ✅ Heat input rate: $Q_{tot} = \dfrac{2 \pi N \mu}{60}(F_{sh}R_{sh} + F_p R_p)$; useful = $\eta Q_{tot}$ with $\eta \approx 0.85$.
- ✅ Heat input per unit length: $E_{line} = \dfrac{Q_{useful}}{v}$ (J/m) — **always divide by v**.
- ✅ Shoulder pressure: $P_{sh} = \dfrac{4 F_{sh}}{\pi (D_{sh}^2 - d_p^2)}$.
- ✅ Effective strain rate in SZ: $\dot{\varepsilon} = \dfrac{\pi N r_p}{30 L_p \sqrt{3}}$ — order of **10¹–10² s⁻¹** (hot-forging regime).
- ✅ Tangential tool velocity at shoulder edge: $V_{tan} = \pi N D_{sh}/60$.
- ✅ **Bobbin / stationary-shoulder tools** are used for thick-plate butt welds and lap joints.
- ✅ **PCBN tools** are mandatory for welding **steels and titanium** (above 900 °C tool tip).
- ✅ Scroll and fluted shoulders/pins improve **material pumping** and **defect-free flow**.
- ✅ Inadequate flow → tunnel, lazy S, kissing bond, flash, surface galling.
- ✅ Examiner's hot words to use: *"viscoplastic flow", "simple shear", "stir zone", "onion ring", "forging consolidation", "advancing vs. retreating side"*.
<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: Welding Environment, Equipment Used, Process Parameters and Characteristics
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PEMET416 - ADVANCED METAL JOINING TECHNIQUES
> - **Module:** Module 3
> - **Topic:** Welding Environment, Equipment Used, Process Parameters, and Characteristics

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Welding Environment — Formal Definition

In the context of **PEMET416 (Advanced Metal Joining Techniques)** and per the KTU 2024 Scheme syllabus, the **welding environment** refers to the complete set of ambient conditions, atmospheric composition, spatial constraints, and protective measures that surround a welding operation. It encompasses three primary domains:

1. **Atmospheric Environment** — The composition of gases (active, inert, reducing) surrounding the arc and weld pool.
2. **Physical Environment** — Workshop conditions including temperature, humidity, ventilation, lighting, and spatial access (indoor vs. field/outdoor).
3. **Human & Safety Environment** — Protection against fumes, UV radiation, spatter, electric shock, and noise through PPE and exhaust systems.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight (Module 3):** The welding environment directly governs the **weld metallurgy**. Contaminants such as **O₂, H₂, and N₂** above threshold limits (typically **>50 ppm** for oxygen in TIG/GTAW) cause porosity, embrittlement, and loss of corrosion resistance. Hence, environment control is **not optional** — it is a metallurgical requirement.

### 1.2 Equipment Used — Formal Definition

**Welding equipment** denotes the integrated set of hardware required to deliver controlled thermal energy, filler material, shielding medium, and motion to produce a sound weld joint. For arc welding processes (the focus of Module 3), the equipment chain typically includes:

- **Power Source** (Transformer, Rectifier, Inverter)
- **Wire Feeder Unit** (for semi-automatic/automatic processes)
- **Welding Torch / Electrode Holder / Gun**
- **Shielding Gas Supply** (Cylinder, Regulator, Flowmeter, Hose)
- **Cooling System** (Water or air-cooled)
- **Ground Clamp & Cables**
- **Positioner / Manipulator / Robot** (for automation)

### 1.3 Process Parameters & Characteristics — Formal Definition

**Process Parameters** are the operator-controllable inputs that govern heat generation, material transfer, and bead formation. The four primary parameters in arc welding are:

| Parameter | Symbol | Typical Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Welding Current | $I$ | Amperes (A) |
| Arc Voltage | $V$ | Volts (V) |
| Travel Speed | $S$ | mm/min or m/min |
| Wire Feed Rate | $WFR$ | m/min |

**Welding Characteristics** are the *outputs* (responses) produced by the interaction of parameters with the environment. They include **Heat Input (HI)**, **Deposition Rate (DR)**, **Penetration**, **Bead Width**, **Reinforcement**, and **Mechanical Properties** of the weld.

### 1.4 Intuitive Analogy — "The Welding Kitchen"

> [!NOTE]
> **Conceptual Analogy: Welding is like Cooking a Controlled Fire**

Imagine you are cooking a delicate dish (the weld) on a gas stove (the welding arc) in your kitchen (the welding environment).

- **The Environment (Kitchen):** A clean, draft-free kitchen with proper exhaust (shielding gas + ventilation) prevents the dish from getting contaminated by dust or smoke. A messy kitchen (poor environment) ruins the dish (porous weld).
- **The Equipment (Stove & Utensils):** You need a reliable gas cylinder (shielding gas cylinder), a burner knob (power source), a regulator (gas regulator), and the right pan (torch). Cheap equipment = uneven flame (unstable arc).
- **The Parameters (Recipe):** Flame intensity (current), flame distance (voltage), stirring speed (travel speed), and ingredient addition rate (wire feed speed). Too much heat or too slow stirring overcooks the food (excessive HAZ, distortion).
- **The Characteristics (Taste & Appearance):** The final dish has tenderness (toughness), color (bead appearance), thickness (deposition), and aroma (mechanical properties).

Just as a master chef controls all four dimensions simultaneously, a welding engineer must harmonize environment, equipment, parameters, and characteristics to produce a **defect-free, mechanically sound weld**.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Welding Environment — Detailed Breakdown

#### A. Atmospheric Environment (Shielding Gas Composition)

The shielding gas serves three critical functions:
1. **Excludes atmospheric gases** (O₂, N₂, H₂) from the arc and molten pool.
2. **Stabilizes the arc** by providing ionizable media.
3. **Influences metal transfer mode** and penetration profile.

**Common Shielding Gases & Their Roles:**

- **Argon (Ar):** Inert, used for TIG/GTAW and MIG/GMAW of stainless steel, aluminum. Pure argon gives **deep, narrow penetration** (cathode cleaning effect on Al).
- **Helium (He):** Inert, hotter arc (~**3000 °C** higher than Ar), used for high-speed welding and thick aluminum sections.
- **CO₂:** Active/reactive gas, used in MIG of mild steel. Produces **deep penetration** but higher spatter.
- **O₂ (2–5%):** Active additive to Ar for MIG of stainless/low-alloy steel to stabilize arc and improve wetting.
- **Ar + CO₂ mixtures:** Most common for mild steel MIG (e.g., **80% Ar + 20% CO₂** called "Corgon"; 92% Ar + 8% CO₂ called "C8").
- **Ar + He mixtures:** For high-quality stainless and nickel alloys.
- **Forming Gas (N₂ + H₂):** Used in plasma welding of stainless steel.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Moisture Control:** Shielding gas dew point must be maintained **below −40 °C** for critical applications (e.g., nuclear, aerospace). Moisture dissociation produces hydrogen, causing **hydrogen-induced cracking (HIC)** and **underbead cracking**.

#### B. Physical Environment Categories

| Environment Type | Description | Typical Process Selection |
|---|---|---|
| **Workshop (Indoor)** | Controlled ventilation, fixed positioners, lighting | All processes; preferred for quality-critical welds |
| **Site (Outdoor)** | Wind, rain, dust, temperature variation | Stick (SMAW) preferred; Flux-cored (FCAW) self-shielded variants |
| **Underwater** | Hyperbaric chamber or wet welding | Hyperbaric TIG/MIG; wet SMAW with special electrodes |
| **Space / Vacuum** | No atmosphere | Electron beam, laser, or TIG with local gas shroud |
| **Nuclear / Hazardous** | Remote manipulation mandatory | Remote TIG, laser, or orbital GTAW |

#### C. Human & Safety Environment

- **Fume Extraction:** Welding fumes contain **Mn, Cr, Ni, fluorides, ozone (O₃), NOₓ**. OSHA PEL for Mn = **5 mg/m³ (ceiling)**.
- **UV/IR Protection:** Arc emits UV-B/UV-C causing **arc eye (photokeratitis)**; auto-darkening helmets (shade 9–13) mandatory.
- **Ventilation:** General ventilation **≥ 2000 ft³/min per welder** for non-toxic processes; local exhaust for toxic fume-producing processes.
- **Electrical Safety:** Open-circuit voltage (OCV) typically **60–80 V (DC)** or **50 V (AC)** — must be limited per safety standards.

---

### 2.2 Equipment Used — Detailed Functional Breakdown

#### A. Power Sources

The power source converts mains AC (typically **415 V, 3-phase, 50 Hz** in India) into a controlled welding output.

| Type | Principle | Advantages | Efficiency |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Transformer (AC)** | Steps down voltage; iron core + copper coil | Rugged, cheap, simple | 60–70% |
| **Engine-Driven Generator** | Diesel engine + DC generator | Portable, field use | 50–60% |
| **Rectifier** | Transformer + diode bridge → DC output | Stable DC arc, smoother | 70–80% |
| **Inverter (IGBT/MOSFET)** | High-freq switching (20–100 kHz) → small transformer → rectified | Lightweight, precise control, high power factor | 85–92% |

> [!NOTE]
> **Modern Trend:** IGBT-based inverter power sources dominate industry. A **400 A inverter** weighs **~25 kg**, while a comparable transformer-rectifier weighs **~150 kg**.

**Static Characteristics of Power Sources:**
- **Constant Current (CC):** Used for Stick (SMAW) and TIG. Voltage varies with arc length; current nearly constant. Drooping V-I curve.
- **Constant Voltage (CV):** Used for MIG, FCAW, SAW. Current varies with feed speed; voltage nearly constant. Flat V-I curve.

#### B. Wire Feeder Unit

For semi-automatic MIG/FCAW:
- **Push-Type Feeder:** Feeder is in the power source; gun pushes wire over **3–5 m**. Suitable for thin wires (0.6–1.2 mm).
- **Spool Gun:** Small spool on the gun; for soft wires like aluminum to prevent buckling.
- **Push-Pull System:** Separate drive rolls near gun; for aluminum wires up to **10–15 m**.

Wire feed rate (WFR) is the **primary current-setting knob** in CV MIG welding: more wire = more current = more heat.

#### C. Shielding Gas Delivery System

$$\text{Cylinder} \rightarrow \text{Regulator (2-stage)} \rightarrow \text{Flowmeter} \rightarrow \text{Gas Hose} \rightarrow \text{Torch Nozzle}$$

- **Regulator:** Reduces cylinder pressure (~**150 bar** for full Ar cylinder) to working pressure (~**2–4 bar**).
- **Flowmeter:** Measures gas flow; typical MIG flow **12–18 L/min**, TIG **7–12 L/min**.

#### D. Welding Torch / Gun

- **Air-Cooled:** For currents up to ~**200–250 A** (MIG) or ~**150 A** (TIG).
- **Water-Cooled:** For high-current TIG (**>200 A**) and heavy MIG (**>300 A**); uses circulating chilled water (~**5 L/min**).

---

### 2.3 Process Parameters — Detailed Hierarchy

The parameters are categorized as:

**Primary (Electrical) Parameters:**
- Welding Current ($I$) — controls **heat generation** and **deposition rate**.
- Arc Voltage ($V$) — controls **arc length** and **bead width**.

**Secondary (Mechanical) Parameters:**
- Travel Speed ($S$) — controls **heat input per unit length**.
- Wire Feed Rate ($WFR$) — coupled with current in CV MIG.
- Electrode Extension / Stick-Out — affects **resistive heating (I²R)** of the electrode.

**Gas Parameter:**
- Shielding Gas Flow Rate ($Q$) — typically **12–18 L/min** for MIG, **7–12 L/min** for TIG.

---

### 2.4 Welding Characteristics — Detailed Analysis

**Heat Input (HI)** is the most critical derived characteristic, defined as the energy delivered per unit length of weld:

$$HI = \frac{\eta \cdot V \cdot I}{S \cdot 1000}$$

Where:
- $HI$ = Heat Input in **kJ/mm**
- $\eta$ = Arc efficiency factor (dimensionless): Stick = **0.75**, TIG = **0.60**, MIG = **0.80**, SAW = **0.90**, Plasma = **0.60**
- $V$ = Arc voltage in **V**
- $I$ = Welding current in **A**
- $S$ = Travel speed in **mm/s**

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Significance of Heat Input:** It directly governs **penetration**, **HAZ width**, **cooling rate**, **grain size**, and **mechanical properties**. Excessive HI causes **coarse grain, reduced toughness, distortion**. Insufficient HI causes **lack of fusion, lack of penetration, porosity**.

---

### 2.5 KTU Formula Sheet (High-Yield Quick Reference)

| # | Formula | Description | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $HI = \dfrac{\eta \cdot V \cdot I}{S \cdot 1000}$ | Heat Input | kJ/mm |
| 2 | $DR = \dfrac{WFR \cdot A_w \cdot \rho}{10^6}$ | Deposition Rate (mass per time) | kg/h |
| 3 | $P_{\text{arc}} = V \cdot I$ | Arc Power | W |
| 4 | $Q_{\text{shield}} = \text{Flow} \times \text{Time}$ | Shielding Gas Consumption | L |
| 5 | $A_w = \pi \cdot \dfrac{d^2}{4}$ | Cross-sectional area of wire (mm²) | mm² |
| 6 | $t_{\text{cool}} \propto \dfrac{1}{(T_8/5)^n}$ | Cooling time relation | s |
| 7 | $E_{\text{elec}} = I^2 \cdot R \cdot L_{\text{ext}}$ | Resistive heat in stick-out | J |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Critical Note on Heat Input:** The factor of **1000** in the denominator converts W·s/mm to kJ/mm (since $1 \text{ W·s} = 1 \text{ J}$ and $1 \text{ kJ} = 1000 \text{ J}$). If $S$ is in **mm/min**, divide by **60** instead of **1000**.

---

### 2.6 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Shipbuilding & Pressure Vessels:** Strict HI limits (e.g., **≤ 2.0 kJ/mm** for thick-plate C-Mn steel) per **AWS D1.1** and **EN 10164** to ensure adequate CTOD toughness.
- **Pipeline Welding (API 1104):** Cellulosic electrodes (E6010) give deep penetration; precise HI control prevents HAZ softening.
- **Aerospace (Ti, Ni Alloys):** Inert chamber welding with O₂ < **50 ppm**, H₂O < **−60 °C** dew point.
- **Automotive Robotic MIG:** Constant-voltage inverter with synergic control matches WFR and voltage automatically.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation of Heat Input Expression

The fundamental definition of **Heat Input** emerges from the energy conservation principle applied to the moving arc.

**Step 1: Define Arc Power**

The instantaneous thermal power generated by the arc is the product of arc voltage and welding current:

$$P_{\text{arc}} = V \cdot I$$

Where $V$ is in volts and $I$ is in amperes, giving $P_{\text{arc}}$ in **watts (W)** or **Joules/second (J/s)**.

**Step 2: Account for Process Efficiency**

Not all arc power is transferred to the workpiece. A fraction is lost via **radiation**, **convection**, **spatter**, and **fume**. The **arc efficiency** $\eta$ accounts for this:

$$P_{\text{effective}} = \eta \cdot V \cdot I$$

**Step 3: Energy Delivered per Unit Length**

If the arc travels along the joint at a constant speed $S$, the time spent depositing energy over a length $L$ is:

$$t = \frac{L}{S}$$

The total energy deposited over length $L$ is:

$$E_{\text{total}} = P_{\text{effective}} \cdot t = \eta \cdot V \cdot I \cdot \frac{L}{S}$$

**Step 4: Heat Input per Unit Length**

Dividing total energy by length $L$:

$$HI = \frac{E_{\text{total}}}{L} = \frac{\eta \cdot V \cdot I}{S}$$

This yields units of **J/mm**. To convert to **kJ/mm**:

$$HI = \frac{\eta \cdot V \cdot I}{S \cdot 1000}$$

This is the canonical heat input formula used across **AWS, ISO, EN, and ASME** codes.

> [!NOTE]
> **Convention on Units:** If $S$ is expressed in **mm/min**, then the formula becomes $HI = \dfrac{\eta \cdot V \cdot I \cdot 60}{S_{\text{mm/min}} \cdot 1000}$ because we must convert minutes to seconds.

---

### 3.2 Analytical Worked Example — Heat Input Calculation

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Style Problem:** A MIG weld is made on a **10 mm thick mild steel plate** using the following parameters: $V = 24 \text{ V}$, $I = 220 \text{ A}$, $S = 5 \text{ mm/s}$. Given MIG arc efficiency $\eta = 0.80$, calculate the heat input and comment on its suitability for the application.

**Solution:**

$$\begin{aligned}
HI &= \frac{\eta \cdot V \cdot I}{S \cdot 1000} \\
&= \frac{0.80 \times 24 \times 220}{5 \times 1000} \\
&= \frac{0.80 \times 5280}{5000} \\
&= \frac{4224}{5000} \\
&= 0.8448 \text{ kJ/mm}
\end{aligned}$$

Converting to kJ/m:

$$HI = 0.8448 \times 1000 = 844.8 \text{ kJ/m}$$

**Comment:** For **10 mm** mild steel plate, a typical recommended heat input range is **1.0–1.5 kJ/mm** for multi-pass welding. At **0.8448 kJ/mm**, the heat input is on the lower side. This may result in:
- Faster cooling rate → harder HAZ
- Possible lack of fusion if root gap/tolerance is tight
- Lower distortion, which is favorable for thin sections

**Recommendation:** Either **increase current to ~280 A** or **reduce travel speed to ~3.5 mm/s** to bring HI into the 1.0–1.2 kJ/mm optimum range.

---

### 3.3 Deposition Rate Derivation

**Step 1: Wire Volume per Unit Time**

If wire feed rate is $WFR$ (in m/min) and wire diameter is $d$ (in mm), the cross-sectional area of the wire is:

$$A_w = \frac{\pi d^2}{4} \quad [\text{mm}^2]$$

The volume of wire fed per minute is:

$$\text{Vol}_{\text{per min}} = WFR \times A_w \quad [\text{mm}^3/\text{min}]$$

Converting WFR from m/min to mm/min: $WFR_{\text{mm}} = WFR \times 1000$.

$$\text{Vol}_{\text{per min}} = WFR \times 1000 \times \frac{\pi d^2}{4} \quad [\text{mm}^3/\text{min}]$$

**Step 2: Mass per Unit Time (Deposition Rate)**

Multiplying by filler metal density $\rho$ (typical for steel: $\rho = 7.85 \text{ g/cm}^3 = 7.85 \times 10^{-3} \text{ g/mm}^3$):

$$DR = WFR \times 1000 \times \frac{\pi d^2}{4} \times \rho \quad [\text{g/min}]$$

To convert to **kg/h**:

$$DR = \frac{WFR \times 1000 \times \frac{\pi d^2}{4} \times \rho \times 60}{10^6} \quad [\text{kg/h}]$$

This simplifies to:

$$DR = \frac{WFR \times \pi \cdot d^2 \cdot \rho}{66.67} \quad [\text{kg/h}]$$

Or, using $WFR$ in m/min and $d$ in mm with $\rho$ in kg/m³:

$$DR_{\text{kg/h}} = \frac{WFR \cdot \pi \cdot d^2 \cdot \rho}{4 \times 10^6 \times 60} \times 3600 = \frac{WFR \cdot \pi \cdot d^2 \cdot \rho}{66.67 \times 10^3}$$

---

### 3.4 Worked Example — Deposition Rate

**Problem:** Calculate the deposition rate for a **MIG welding** operation using **1.2 mm** diameter steel wire fed at **8 m/min**. Steel density $\rho = 7850 \text{ kg/m}^3$.

$$\begin{aligned}
A_w &= \frac{\pi (1.2 \times 10^{-3})^2}{4} = \frac{\pi \times 1.44 \times 10^{-6}}{4} = 1.131 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2 \\
\text{Vol/min} &= WFR \times A_w = 8 \times 1.131 \times 10^{-6} = 9.05 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3/\text{min} \\
\text{Mass/min} &= 9.05 \times 10^{-6} \times 7850 = 0.0710 \text{ kg/min} \\
DR &= 0.0710 \times 60 = 4.26 \text{ kg/h}
\end{aligned}$$

**Result:** $DR = 4.26 \text{ kg/h}$ (assuming **100% deposition efficiency**; actual deposition efficiency for MIG is ~**95–98%**, so realistic $DR \approx 4.05 \text{ kg/h}$).

---

### 3.5 Analytical Matrix — Parameter–Characteristic Relationship

This matrix maps the qualitative effect of **increasing** each parameter on each welding characteristic.

| Parameter ↑ | HI | Penetration | Bead Width | DR | Distortion | HAZ Width |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Current ($I$) ↑ | ↑ | ↑↑ | ↑ | ↑↑ | ↑ | ↑ |
| Voltage ($V$) ↑ | ↑ | ↑ (mild) | ↑↑ | ↑ | ↑ | ↑ |
| Travel Speed ($S$) ↑ | ↓ | ↓ | ↓ | — | ↓ | ↓ |
| Wire Feed Rate ↑ | ↑ | ↑ | ↑ | ↑↑ | ↑ | ↑ |
| Gas Flow ($Q$) ↑ | — | ↑ (until optimum, then ↓) | — | — | — | — |
| Stick-Out ↑ | ↑ | ↑ (then ↓) | ↑ | ↑ | ↑ | ↑ |

**Reading the Matrix:**
- Increasing **current** has the **strongest effect on penetration** — current density governs arc constriction and electromagnetic pinch force.
- Increasing **voltage** primarily **widens the bead** by lengthening the arc.
- Increasing **travel speed** reduces HI, producing **narrower, deeper-looking** beads but with **less fusion** risk.

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Student Mistake:** Confusing *Voltage* effect on penetration. Many students incorrectly believe higher voltage gives more penetration. **Reality:** Voltage primarily widens the bead; **current** drives penetration.

---

### 3.6 Cooling Rate & HAZ Relationship

The **cooling time between 800 °C and 500 °C** ($t_{8/5}$) is a critical metallurgical parameter that determines HAZ microstructure:

$$t_{8/5} = \frac{HI^2}{2\pi \lambda \rho c (T_1 - T_0)^2} \cdot \frac{1}{d}$$

Where:
- $\lambda$ = thermal conductivity (W/m·K)
- $\rho$ = density (kg/m³)
- $c$ = specific heat (J/kg·K)
- $T_1$ = **800 °C** (above which austenite exists)
- $T_0$ = **500 °C** (below which bainite/martensite formation completes for many steels)
- $d$ = plate thickness (mm)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Engineering Implication:** Higher HI → longer $t_{8/5}$ → coarser grain → lower toughness. Codes (e.g., EN 10164) often prescribe **maximum t₈/₅** values for given steel grades and thicknesses.

---

### 3.7 Empirical Penetration Equation (Lancaster Correlation)

For a moving arc on a plate, penetration depth $P$ can be estimated by:

$$P \approx k \cdot \sqrt{\frac{HI}{d \cdot \rho c (T_m - T_0)}}$$

Where:
- $k$ = dimensionless constant (~0.5–1.0)
- $T_m$ = melting temperature of base metal
- $T_0$ = initial plate temperature (preheat)

This shows **penetration increases with the square root of heat input** but inversely with **plate thickness** — explaining why thick plates need **proportionally higher current or multiple passes**.
<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
## SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Functional Architecture of a Complete MIG/GMAW Welding Station

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Mains["Mains Supply 415V 3 Phase 50Hz"] --> Inverter["IGBT Inverter Power Source CV Mode"]
    Inverter -->|Welding Cable| WireFeed["Wire Feeder Unit Push Type"]
    Inverter -->|Control Cable| WireFeed
    WireFeed -->|Wire 1.2mm| Torch["MIG Torch Air Cooled"]
    GasCyl["Shielding Gas Cylinder Argon or ArCO2 Mix 200 bar"] --> Reg["Two Stage Regulator"]
    Reg --> Flow["Flowmeter 12 to 18 L per min"]
    Flow --> Hose["Gas Hose"]
    Hose --> Torch
    Torch -->|Arc + Shielded Droplet Transfer| WeldPool["Weld Pool on Workpiece"]
    Workpiece["Workpiece Mild Steel Plate"] --> WeldPool
    Workpiece --> Ground["Earth Clamp"]
    Ground --> Inverter
    Fume["Fume Extraction Hood"] -.Fumes.-> WeldPool
    PPE["PPE Helmet Gloves Apron"] -.Protects.-> Welder[Welder Operator]
    Welder -.Controls.-> Inverter
    Welder -.Adjusts.-> Flow
```

### 4.2 Block Diagram — Relationship of Inputs, Process, and Outputs

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Inputs["Process Inputs - Controllable Parameters"]
        P1["Welding Current I"]
        P2["Arc Voltage V"]
        P3["Travel Speed S"]
        P4["Wire Feed Rate"]
        P5["Shielding Gas Flow"]
    end

    subgraph Environment["Welding Environment"]
        E1["Atmosphere - Wind Humidity"]
        E2["Shielding Gas Composition"]
        E3["Base Metal Temperature Preheat"]
        E4["Joint Geometry Fit up"]
    end

    subgraph Equipment["Equipment Chain"]
        Q1["Power Source CC or CV"]
        Q2["Wire Feeder"]
        Q3["Torch and Nozzle"]
        Q4["Gas Delivery"]
    end

    subgraph Process["Arc Welding Process"]
        X1["Arc Generation"]
        X2["Metal Transfer"]
        X3["Weld Pool Solidification"]
    end

    subgraph Outputs["Welding Characteristics"]
        O1["Heat Input HI kJ per mm"]
        O2["Penetration Depth"]
        O3["Bead Width and Height"]
        O4["Deposition Rate"]
        O5["HAZ Microstructure"]
        O6["Mechanical Properties UTS Toughness Hardness"]
        O7["Distortion and Residual Stress"]
    end

    Inputs --> Process
    Environment --> Process
    Equipment --> Process
    Process --> Outputs
    O1 --> O5
    O1 --> O6
    O1 --> O7
    O2 --> O6
    O3 --> O6
    O4 --> O7
```

### 4.3 Decision Flow — Selecting Process Parameters

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start["Start: Define Base Material and Thickness"] --> Q1{"Material Type"}
    Q1 -->|Mild Steel| A["Process: MIG or FCAW or SAW"]
    Q1 -->|Stainless Steel| B["Process: TIG or MIG with Ar plus 2 percent O2"]
    Q1 -->|Aluminum| C["Process: TIG AC or MIG with Pure Ar"]
    Q1 -->|Titanium| D["Process: TIG with Trailing Shield in Argon Chamber"]

    A --> P1["Set Voltage 20 to 28 V"]
    P1 --> P2["Set Current based on Wire Feed Rate"]
    P2 --> P3["Set Travel Speed to achieve Heat Input 1.0 to 1.5 kJ per mm"]
    P3 --> P4["Set Shielding Gas Flow 14 to 18 L per min"]
    P4 --> Check{"Verify Bead Appearance and Penetration"}
    Check -->|Undercut or Lack of Fusion| Fix1["Reduce Travel Speed or Increase Current"]
    Check -->|Porosity| Fix2["Check Gas Flow and Wind Drafts"]
    Check -->|Excessive Spatter| Fix3["Adjust Voltage or Switch to Gas Mix"]
    Fix1 --> Check
    Fix2 --> Check
    Fix3 --> Check
    Check -->|Acceptable| Done["Document WPS and PQR"]
```

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
## SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

> **Question A1:** Define **welding environment** and list **any four factors** that affect weld quality.
> `[KTU University Exam - May 2024, Module 3]`

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

**Definition (1 mark):** The welding environment is the set of ambient conditions — atmospheric, physical, and human/safety — that surrounds and influences the welding operation.

**Four factors affecting weld quality (2 marks — 0.5 each):**
1. **Atmospheric contamination** — O₂, N₂, H₂ ingress causing porosity and embrittlement.
2. **Humidity** — moisture in shielding gas or electrode coating → hydrogen porosity.
3. **Wind/drafts** — disperse shielding gas, especially critical above **5 km/h** wind speed.
4. **Ambient temperature** — affects cooling rate and preheat requirements.
5. *(Optional 5th)* — ventilation affecting fume extraction and welder comfort.

---

> **Question A2:** What is **arc efficiency**? State the typical efficiency values for **SMAW, GTAW, GMAW, and SAW**.
> `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Module 3]`

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

**Definition (1 mark):** Arc efficiency ($\eta$) is the ratio of heat actually delivered to the workpiece to the total electrical energy input in the arc, expressed as a decimal fraction.

**Typical values (2 marks — 0.5 each):**
| Process | Arc Efficiency ($\eta$) |
|---|---|
| SMAW (Stick) | **0.75** |
| GTAW (TIG) | **0.60** |
| GMAW (MIG/MAG) | **0.80** |
| SAW (Submerged Arc) | **0.90** |

---

### 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks with Internal Choice)

> **Question B — Choice A:** Explain in detail the **welding environment** with reference to **(a)** atmospheric and shielding gas requirements, and **(b)** the various categories of welding equipment used in arc welding processes.
> `[KTU University Exam - May 2024, Module 3]`

#### Part (a) — Atmospheric and Shielding Gas Requirements (7 marks)

**1. Role of Atmosphere (2 marks):**
The surrounding atmosphere contains **O₂ (~21%), N₂ (~78%), H₂O, CO₂** which are **harmful** to the molten weld pool. They cause:
- **Porosity** (gas pockets)
- **Oxidation** (slag inclusions, loss of alloying elements)
- **Nitrogen embrittlement** (in steels, forms brittle nitrides)
- **Hydrogen cracking** (cold cracking, delayed cracking)

**2. Shielding Gas Functions (2 marks):**
- **Exclusion** of atmospheric gases from arc and weld pool
- **Arc stabilization** by providing ionizable species
- **Heat transfer modification** (Ar → constricted arc; He → wider, hotter arc)
- **Metal transfer mode control** (e.g., Ar/CO₂ gives spray transfer at higher currents)

**3. Common Shielding Gas Compositions (2 marks):**
- **Pure Ar** → TIG of Al, stainless; MIG of Al (deep penetration)
- **Pure CO₂** → MIG of mild steel (cheap, deep penetration, high spatter)
- **80% Ar + 20% CO₂** → general mild steel MIG (balanced)
- **98% Ar + 2% O₂** → stainless steel MIG (stable arc, clean weld)
- **75% Ar + 25% He** → high-speed TIG of stainless & Ni alloys
- **Forming gas (90% N₂ + 10% H₂)** → plasma welding of stainless

**4. Quality Control of Shielding Gas (1 mark):**
- Dew point **< −40 °C**
- Purity **≥ 99.99%** for critical welds
- Flow rate **12–18 L/min** for MIG; **7–12 L/min** for TIG
- Hose integrity; no leaks at fittings

#### Part (b) — Categories of Welding Equipment (7 marks)

**1. Power Source (2 marks):**
- **Transformer:** AC output; rugged, used for stick/TIG
- **Rectifier:** Transformer + diode bridge → DC; smoother arc
- **Inverter (IGBT):** High-frequency switching → compact, precise; modern industry standard
- **Engine-driven generator:** Portable; field use

**2. Static Characteristics (1 mark):**
- **Constant Current (CC):** SMAW, GTAW; drooping curve
- **Constant Voltage (CV):** GMAW, FCAW, SAW; flat curve

**3. Wire Feeder Unit (1.5 marks):**
- **Push type** — feeder in power source, for short gun (<5 m)
- **Pull type** — motor in gun
- **Push-pull type** — both, for soft Al wires (long distances)
- **Spool gun** — for Al, soft wires, prevents bird-nesting

**4. Shielding Gas Delivery System (1.5 marks):**
- Cylinder → 2-stage regulator → flowmeter → hose → torch nozzle
- 2-stage regulator ensures constant flow despite cylinder pressure drop

**5. Torch and Cooling (1 mark):**
- **Air-cooled:** MIG up to ~250 A; TIG up to ~150 A
- **Water-cooled:** for high-current operations (>250 A MIG, >200 A TIG)

> [!WARNING]
> **Examiner's Pitfall Callout:**
> 1. Students often **omit the difference between CC and CV** power sources — losing 1 mark. Always state which process uses which.
> 2. Do NOT confuse **shielding gas flow rate** with **pressure**. Pressure is regulated in bar; flow in L/min.
> 3. For MIG, mention **constant voltage** explicitly; for TIG/Stick, mention **constant current** explicitly.

---

> **Question B — Choice B:** Discuss in detail the **(a)** primary welding process parameters and their effects on weld characteristics, and **(b)** the concept of **heat input** with a worked numerical example suitable for a **10 mm thick mild steel plate**.
> `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Module 3]`

#### Part (a) — Process Parameters and Their Effects (7 marks)

**1. Primary Parameters Defined (2 marks):**

- **Welding Current ($I$, A):** Governs heat generation, penetration depth, and deposition rate. Higher current → deeper penetration, higher deposition.
- **Arc Voltage ($V$, V):** Determines arc length and bead width. Higher voltage → wider, flatter bead with more spatter risk.
- **Travel Speed ($S$, mm/s or mm/min):** Speed of arc travel along the joint. Higher speed → less heat per unit length, narrower bead.
- **Wire Feed Rate ($WFR$, m/min):** In MIG, directly coupled with current in CV mode. Higher WFR → higher current and higher deposition.

**2. Effects on Weld Characteristics (3 marks):**

| Parameter ↑ | Penetration | Bead Width | HI | DR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Current ↑ | ↑↑↑ (strong) | ↑ | ↑ | ↑↑↑ |
| Voltage ↑ | ↑ (mild) | ↑↑ (strong) | ↑ | ↑ |
| Travel Speed ↑ | ↓ | ↓ | ↓↓ (strong) | — |

**Key Insights:**
- **Current** dominates penetration via electromagnetic pinch force.
- **Voltage** dominates bead width via arc spread.
- **Travel speed** inversely affects HI most strongly.
- Increasing **stick-out** (electrode extension) raises deposition through resistive heating: $E = I^2 R t$.

**3. Secondary Parameters (2 marks):**
- **Electrode polarity** — DCEP for most arc welding; DCEN for TIG of aluminum (provides cathodic cleaning).
- **Torch angle** — push angle (10–20° forward) gives deeper penetration; drag angle gives wider bead.
- **Gas flow rate** — too low → porosity; too high → turbulence and air ingress.

#### Part (b) — Heat Input Concept and Worked Example (7 marks)

**1. Definition of Heat Input (2 marks):**
Heat Input is the **arc energy transferred to the workpiece per unit length of weld**, accounting for the process efficiency. It governs HAZ microstructure, mechanical properties, and distortion.

$$HI = \frac{\eta \cdot V \cdot I}{S \cdot 1000} \quad [\text{kJ/mm}]$$

**2. Significance (2 marks):**
- Controls **HAZ width, grain size, and toughness**
- Higher HI → softer, coarser HAZ (lower strength, lower toughness)
- Lower HI → harder, possibly brittle HAZ; risk of lack of fusion
- Codes specify maximum HI for given material/thickness (e.g., AWS D1.1, EN 10164)

**3. Worked Example (3 marks):**

> A MIG weld on **10 mm mild steel** uses $V = 25 \text{ V}$, $I = 240 \text{ A}$, $S = 4 \text{ mm/s}$. Given $\eta = 0.80$, calculate the heat input.

$$\begin{aligned}
HI &= \frac{0.80 \times 25 \times 240}{4 \times 1000} \\
&= \frac{4800}{4000} \\
&= 1.2 \text{ kJ/mm}
\end{aligned}$$

**Result:** $HI = 1.2 \text{ kJ/mm}$ — within the acceptable range of **1.0–1.5 kJ/mm** for 10 mm mild steel multi-pass welding.

**Discussion:** This HI yields a balanced HAZ with adequate toughness, minimal distortion, and good fusion. For higher productivity, increasing current to **280 A** while keeping speed at **4 mm/s** would give $HI = 1.4 \text{ kJ/mm}$ — pushing toward the upper limit.

> [!WARNING]
> **Examiner's Pitfall Callout:**
> 1. **Unit conversion trap:** If $S$ is in mm/min, formula becomes $HI = \dfrac{\eta \cdot V \cdot I \cdot 60}{S_{\text{mm/min}} \cdot 1000}$. Many students forget this and lose 1–2 marks.
> 2. **Efficiency omission:** Always include $\eta$ in the calculation. Without it, the value is **arc energy**, not **heat input**.
> 3. **Confusion with travel direction:** Mention if it's single-pass or multi-pass; multi-pass welds have **interpass temperature** control which effectively resets the HI per pass.

---

### 5.3 KTU Quick-Reference Summary Table

| Term | Definition | Typical Value |
|---|---|---|
| Heat Input (HI) | Energy per unit length delivered to weld | 0.5–3.0 kJ/mm |
| Arc Efficiency ($\eta$) | Fraction of arc energy reaching workpiece | 0.60–0.90 |
| Deposition Rate (DR) | Mass of filler deposited per unit time | 1–8 kg/h (MIG) |
| Shielding Gas Flow | Volume of protective gas per minute | 7–20 L/min |
| Open Circuit Voltage | No-load voltage of power source | 50–80 V |
| Dew Point | Moisture indicator in shielding gas | ≤ −40 °C |
| Stick-Out | Electrode extension beyond contact tip | 10–25 mm |

---

### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Yield Revision Checklist for KTU Module 3:**

- [x] **Welding environment** = atmospheric + physical + safety domains.
- [x] **Shielding gases**: Pure Ar (TIG, Al, SS), CO₂ (cheap MIG), Ar+CO₂ (general steel), Ar+O₂ (stainless MIG), Ar+He (high-speed SS).
- [x] **Equipment chain**: Power source → Wire feeder → Torch → Gas delivery → Cooling → Earth.
- [x] **Power source types**: Transformer, Rectifier, Inverter (modern, efficient), Engine-driven.
- [x] **CC vs CV**: CC for Stick/TIG; CV for MIG/FCAW/SAW.
- [x] **Four primary parameters**: Current ($I$), Voltage ($V$), Travel Speed ($S$), Wire Feed Rate (WFR).
- [x] **Current controls penetration**; **Voltage controls bead width**; **Travel speed controls HI inversely**.
- [x] **Heat Input formula**: $HI = \dfrac{\eta \cdot V \cdot I}{S \cdot 1000}$ in **kJ/mm** when $S$ is in **mm/s**.
- [x] **Arc efficiency values**: SMAW = 0.75, TIG = 0.60, MIG = 0.80, SAW = 0.90.
- [x] **Dew point** of shielding gas must be **< −40 °C** for critical welds.
- [x] **Push-type wire feeder** for steel up to **5 m**; **push-pull** for aluminum and longer distances.
- [x] **Spool gun** used for soft aluminum wires to prevent bird-nesting.
- [x] **Heat input affects**: HAZ width, grain size, toughness, distortion, residual stress.
- [x] **Codes**: AWS D1.1, ASME IX, EN 10164, API 1104 all prescribe HI limits.
- [x] **Higher HI → coarser grains, lower toughness, more distortion**.
- [x] **Stick-out resistive heating**: $E = I^2 R L_{\text{ext}}$ — increases deposition in MIG.
- [x] **DCEP** is standard for most arc welding; **DCEN** used for TIG aluminum.
- [x] **Cooling time $t_{8/5}$** is a critical metallurgical parameter; controlled by HI and preheat.
- [x] **Penetration** increases with **square root of HI** but decreases with plate thickness.
- [x] Always mention **arc efficiency** explicitly in heat input calculations — examiners penalize its omission.
<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PEMET416 - ADVANCED METAL JOINING TECHNIQUES
> - **Module:** Module 2
> - **Topic:** Weld Joint Design and Applications

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# Weld Joint Design and Applications

## 1. Core Technical Definition

> [!NOTE]
> **Weld Joint Design** is the systematic engineering process of determining the type, size, geometry, and location of welds in a fabricated structure to safely transmit applied loads while satisfying strength, economy, and serviceability requirements under static, dynamic, and environmental conditions.

In the KTU 2024 Scheme framework, weld joint design is treated as an **applied mechanics problem** where the welded joint becomes a critical load-transferring element, and the design must be validated against **allowable stresses** prescribed by codes such as **IS 800:2007**, **AWS D1.1**, and **IS 816:1969**.

### Fundamental Weld Joint Types (AWS / IS Classification)

| Joint Type | Description | Typical Application |
|------------|-------------|---------------------|
| **Butt Joint** | Two plates placed edge-to-edge in the same plane | Pressure vessels, pipelines |
| **Lap Joint** | Two plates overlapping each other | Sheet metal structures |
| **Tee Joint** | Two plates meeting at 90° forming a T | Beam-to-column connections |
| **Corner Joint** | Two plates meeting at right angle at edge | Box sections, frames |
| **Edge Joint** | Two plates placed edge-to-edge, parallel | Sheet metal flooring |

### Fundamental Weld Types

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Fillet Welds** and **Groove Welds** are the two principal weld types used in structural design. Approximately **70% of all structural welds** are fillet welds, making them the most economically significant category.

| Weld Type | Geometry | Primary Loading |
|-----------|----------|-----------------|
| **Fillet Weld** | Triangular cross-section (typically 45°) | Shear |
| **Square Groove Butt** | Plates abutted with no edge preparation | Axial tension/compression |
| **Single-V Groove Butt** | One side beveled (typically 30°) | Heavy plates (>6 mm) |
| **Double-V Groove Butt** | Both sides beveled | Very thick plates (>20 mm) |
| **Plug/Slot Weld** | Filled hole or slot | Stiffener attachment |
| **Spot/Projection Weld** | Resistance welding nugget | Sheet metal assemblies |

### Conceptual Analogy

> [!TIP]
> **Analogy – The Handshake:** Imagine a bolted connection as a "handshake" — discrete contact points transmit load. Now imagine a **welded joint** as a "sealed embrace" — the load is distributed continuously along the entire joint line, just like two hands gripping firmly along their full length. **Weld joint design** is the engineering art of ensuring this "embrace" is strong enough, in the right direction, and at the right place to handle the forces applied. A poorly designed weld is like a weak handshake — it fails at the weakest point under load.

### Key Geometric Parameters

- **Leg Size (s):** The shortest distance from the weld root to the weld face (the two catheti of the triangular cross-section).
- **Throat Thickness (t):** The perpendicular distance from the weld root to the hypotenuse. For an equal-leg 45° fillet: **t = 0.707 × s**.
- **Weld Length (L):** The effective length over which the weld transmits load.
- **Effective Throat Area (A):** A = t × L = 0.707 × s × L.
- **Convexity / Concavity:** Deviation of the weld face from the ideal triangular profile.

> [!NOTE]
> **Standard Weld Sizes (IS 800:2007):** Minimum leg size depends on the thickness of the thicker plate. For plates up to 10 mm thick, minimum fillet leg size = **3 mm**; for 20–32 mm, minimum = **6 mm**; for thicker plates, minimum = **8 mm**. The maximum leg size is limited to **1.5 mm less than the edge thickness** for plates along the edge.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Stresses in Welded Joints

A fillet weld is treated as a line of **uniform strength**, and the load is assumed to be resisted by **shear on the throat area**. This is a simplification that aligns with experimental evidence and is universally adopted by **IS 800:2007** and **AWS D1.1**.

### Failure Modes in Fillet Welds

> [!WARNING]
> **The Throat is the Critical Plane:** A fillet weld ALWAYS fails through the **throat**, not the leg. The throat is the smallest cross-section and lies on the plane of maximum shear stress (45° to both the leg and the weld axis). This is the foundation of all fillet weld design equations.

1. **Throat Shear Failure** — most common, the design basis.
2. **Fusion Zone Failure** — at the weld-parent metal interface (controlled by weld procedure).
3. **Parent Metal Shear / Tear-out** — when weld is too near the edge (controlled by edge distance).
4. **Base Metal Failure** — in the parent material (controlled by plate strength).

### Types of Loading on Fillet Welds

| Loading Type | Description | Critical Stress |
|--------------|-------------|-----------------|
| **Parallel / Longitudinal** | Load parallel to weld axis | Pure shear (τ ∥) |
| **Transverse** | Load perpendicular to weld axis | Combined (higher strength) |
| **Bending** | Moment about weld group centroid | Linear shear distribution |
| **Torsional** | Moment about weld group centroid (in-plane) | Shear + torsion |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Experimental Fact:** A transverse fillet weld is approximately **30% stronger** than a parallel fillet weld of the same size, because the transverse weld develops a component of normal stress on the throat that contributes to the load capacity. The simplified IS 800:2007 design treats both as throat shear, but applies a **higher allowable stress for shop welds** (typically **150 N/mm²** for E41 electrodes, **165 N/mm²** for E43 electrodes at shop) and a lower value for field welds.

## 2.2 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

| # | Formula | Description | Units |
|---|---------|-------------|-------|
| 1 | $t = 0.707 \cdot s$ | Throat thickness from leg size | mm |
| 2 | $A_{throat} = 0.707 \cdot s \cdot L$ | Effective throat area | mm² |
| 3 | $\tau = \dfrac{P}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot L}$ | Average throat shear stress (parallel loading) | N/mm² |
| 4 | $L = \dfrac{P}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot \tau_{allow}}$ | Required weld length for given load | mm |
| 5 | $s = \dfrac{P}{0.707 \cdot L \cdot \tau_{allow}}$ | Required leg size for given load | mm |
| 6 | $\tau_{\perp} = \dfrac{P_{\perp}}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot L}$ | Stress due to perpendicular force | N/mm² |
| 7 | $\tau_{\parallel} = \dfrac{P_{\parallel}}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot L}$ | Stress due to parallel force | N/mm² |
| 8 | $\tau_{resultant} = \sqrt{\tau_{\perp}^{2} + \tau_{\parallel}^{2}}$ | Combined stress (vector sum) | N/mm² |
| 9 | $I_{x} = \sum_{i} (I_{xi} + A_i \cdot y_i^2)$ | Moment of inertia of weld group (parallel axis theorem) | mm⁴ |
| 10 | $I_{p} = I_{x} + I_{y}$ | Polar moment of inertia (for torsion) | mm⁴ |
| 11 | $\tau_{b} = \dfrac{M \cdot c}{I}$ | Bending shear stress in weld | N/mm² |
| 12 | $\tau_{T} = \dfrac{T \cdot r}{I_{p}}$ | Torsional shear stress in weld | N/mm² |
| 13 | $q = \dfrac{P}{L} \pm \dfrac{M \cdot \bar{y}}{I}$ | Linear shear stress (direct + bending) per unit length | N/mm |
| 14 | $f_{wd} = f_{y} / (\gamma_{mw} \cdot \sqrt{3})$ | Design strength of fillet weld (LRFD) | N/mm² |

> [!NOTE]
> **Boundary Conditions to Remember:**
> - Minimum effective weld length ≥ **4 × leg size** (else size governs)
> - Effective length = **Actual length − 2 × leg size** (for end returns/undercuts)
> - Maximum effective length in lap joints ≤ **40 × throat thickness** (to avoid uneven stress distribution)
> - For end-loaded fillet welds (transverse), **end returns** of length ≥ **2s** must be provided to prevent cracking.

## 2.3 Real-World Engineering Utility

Weld joint design is foundational to:
- **Structural steel buildings** (moment connections, beam-column joints)
- **Pressure vessel and boiler fabrication** (ASME Sec. VIII)
- **Bridges and offshore platforms** (cyclic and dynamic loading)
- **Automotive chassis** (resistance spot welds, MIG/MAG robotic welds)
- **Aerospace structures** (FSW of aluminum alloys, laser welding of titanium)
- **Shipbuilding** (submerged arc welding of thick plates)
- **Pipeline construction** (API 1104, circumferential girth welds)

> [!TIP]
> **For KTU Examinations:** Always state the code reference (IS 800 / IS 816) when quoting allowable stresses. Examiners award **2 marks** just for the correct clause and stress value.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation: Throat Thickness of a 45° Fillet Weld

The fillet weld cross-section is an **isosceles right triangle** with both legs equal to the leg size **s**, and the hypotenuse inclined at 45° to each leg.

**Step 1 — Geometry Setup**

Consider the right triangle with legs along the vertical and horizontal faces of the two joined plates, and the hypotenuse forming the weld face.

$$
\text{Legs} = s, \quad \text{Hypotenuse} = s\sqrt{2}
$$

**Step 2 — Identify the Throat**

The throat is the perpendicular from the root (the right-angle vertex) to the hypotenuse.

$$
\text{For an isosceles right triangle: } t = \frac{s \cdot s}{s\sqrt{2}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

**Step 3 — Rationalize the Denominator**

$$
t = \frac{s}{\sqrt{2}} \times \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{s\sqrt{2}}{2} = 0.707 \cdot s
$$

$$
\boxed{\,t = 0.707 \cdot s\,}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Conversion factor 0.707 = sin(45°) = cos(45°) = 1/√2.** This is the most-tested number in weld design problems. Memorize it.

---

## 3.2 Derivation: Shear Stress in a Fillet Weld Carrying a Direct Load

**Step 1 — Consider a Fillet Weld of Leg Size s and Length L**

The throat area resisting the applied shear load P is:

$$
A_{throat} = t \cdot L = 0.707 \cdot s \cdot L
$$

**Step 2 — Apply the Basic Stress Equation**

Average shear stress is force divided by the area resisting it:

$$
\tau = \frac{P}{A_{throat}} = \frac{P}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot L}
$$

**Step 3 — Solve for Required Leg Size**

Rearranging with the allowable shear stress τ_allow:

$$
s = \frac{P}{0.707 \cdot L \cdot \tau_{allow}}
$$

> [!TIP]
> **Worked Insight — Why Throat, Not Leg?** If the weld were checked on the leg, the area would be s × L, giving a higher calculated stress. The throat is the **weakest plane** (smallest area, maximum shear). Designers always use throat area as a **conservative** design basis.

---

## 3.3 Analytical Matrix: Stress Components in Combined Loading

When a fillet weld is subjected to combined forces, the resultant shear stress at any point is the **vector sum** of all components.

### Case A: Direct Shear + Bending (Tee Joint with Eccentric Load)

**Setup:** A bracket welded to a column with vertical load P at eccentricity e from the weld line.

**Step 1 — Direct Shear Component**

$$
q_{direct} = \frac{P}{L} \quad \text{(shear force per unit length, N/mm)}
$$

**Step 2 — Bending Moment Component**

Moment M = P × e. The bending stress at distance y from the centroidal axis:

$$
q_{bending} = \frac{M \cdot y}{I}
$$

**Step 3 — Resultant Shear per Unit Length**

$$
q_{resultant} = \frac{P}{L} \pm \frac{M \cdot y}{I}
$$

**Step 4 — Convert to Throat Shear Stress**

$$
\tau = \frac{q_{resultant}}{0.707 \cdot s}
$$

### Case B: Pure Torsion (C-Shaped Weld Under In-Plane Moment)

**Step 1 — Compute Polar Moment of Inertia of Weld Group**

For a weld line, treat each segment as a line of length L_i at distance r_i from the centroid:

$$
I_{p} = \sum_{i} L_i \cdot r_i^{2}
$$

**Step 2 — Torsional Shear Stress**

$$
\tau_{T} = \frac{T \cdot r_{max}}{I_{p}}
$$

**Step 3 — For Thin Lines (Line Weld Approximation)**

The unit shear force per unit length at any point on the weld:

$$
q = \frac{T \cdot r}{I_{p}}
$$

**Step 4 — Maximum Stress at the Farthest Point**

$$
\tau_{max} = \frac{T \cdot r_{max}}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot I_{p}}
$$

### Case C: Combined Direct + Torsion

For a C-shaped weld carrying a vertical load P at distance e from the centroid:

**Step 1 — Direct Shear (Uniform Distribution)**

$$
q_{v} = \frac{P}{L_{total}} \quad \text{(downward, assumed constant along weld)}
$$

**Step 2 — Torsional Shear (at right angles to radius vector)**

$$
q_{T} = \frac{T \cdot r}{I_{p}} = \frac{P \cdot e \cdot r}{I_{p}}
$$

**Step 3 — Resultant**

$$
q_{R} = \sqrt{q_{v}^{2} + q_{T}^{2}}
$$

**Step 4 — Leg Size Required**

$$
s = \frac{q_{R, max}}{0.707 \cdot \tau_{allow}}
$$

---

## 3.4 Numerical Example: Bracket Welded to Column

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Standard Problem — Practice This Type**

**Given:** A bracket carrying a vertical load P = **80 kN** is welded to a column using two vertical fillet welds of length **150 mm each**, spaced **200 mm apart** (center-to-center). The load is applied at a distance of **250 mm** from the face of the column. Allowable shear stress = **110 N/mm²**. Find the required leg size.

**Solution:**

**Step 1 — Identify the Weld Configuration**

- Total weld length: L = 2 × 150 = **300 mm**
- Weld group treated as two parallel line welds
- Distance from centroid of weld group to each weld: c = 100 mm
- Direct shear: P = 80,000 N

**Step 2 — Calculate Direct Shear Stress**

$$
\tau_{d} = \frac{P}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot L} = \frac{80{,}000}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot 300}
$$

$$
\tau_{d} = \frac{377.3}{s} \quad \text{N/mm}^2
$$

**Step 3 — Calculate Moment of Inertia of Weld Group**

For two parallel line welds:

$$
I = 2 \cdot L_i \cdot c^{2} = 2 \cdot 150 \cdot (100)^{2} = 3{,}000{,}000 \text{ mm}^{3}\text{-equivalent}
$$

**Step 4 — Calculate Bending Moment**

$$
M = P \cdot e = 80{,}000 \cdot 250 = 20{,}000{,}000 \text{ N·mm}
$$

**Step 5 — Calculate Bending Shear Stress**

The bending shear at the extreme weld:

$$
\tau_{b} = \frac{M \cdot c}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot I} = \frac{20{,}000{,}000 \cdot 100}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot 3{,}000{,}000}
$$

$$
\tau_{b} = \frac{943.1}{s} \quad \text{N/mm}^2
$$

**Step 6 — Total Shear Stress (Algebraic Sum)**

$$
\tau_{max} = \frac{377.3}{s} + \frac{943.1}{s} = \frac{1320.4}{s} \quad \text{N/mm}^2
$$

**Step 7 — Equate to Allowable Stress and Solve**

$$
\frac{1320.4}{s} = 110 \quad \Rightarrow \quad s = \frac{1320.4}{110} = 12.0 \text{ mm}
$$

**Step 8 — Adopt Standard Leg Size**

Provide **s = 12 mm** fillet weld (standard sizes: 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20 mm).

$$
\boxed{\,s_{adopted} = 12 \text{ mm}\,}
$$

**Step 9 — Verification of Minimum Length Criterion**

Minimum length = 4 × s = 4 × 12 = 48 mm. Our L = 150 mm > 48 mm ✓

# KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## Part A: Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Q1. [KTU University Exam - May 2024]
**Differentiate between a fillet weld and a butt weld. State the design strength values as per IS 800:2007 for fillet welds using E41 and E43 electrodes.**

**Model Answer:**

| Feature | Fillet Weld | Butt Weld |
|---------|-------------|-----------|
| Cross-section | Triangular (≈45°) | Square / V / U groove |
| Preparation | Not required (lap or T) | Edge preparation needed |
| Load transfer | Shear on throat | Tension / compression on plate |
| Strength | Lower | Higher (full strength) |
| Cost | Economical | Costlier |

As per IS 800:2007, the design strength of a fillet weld (per unit throat area) is:

$$
f_{wd} = \frac{f_u}{\sqrt{3} \cdot \gamma_{mw}}
$$

For **E41 electrodes (f_u = 410 N/mm², γ_mw = 1.25 for shop)**: f_wd ≈ **189 N/mm²**  
For **E43 electrodes (f_u = 430 N/mm², γ_mw = 1.25 for shop)**: f_wd ≈ **198 N/mm²**

---

### Q2. [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]
**What is meant by effective throat thickness? Derive the relationship between throat thickness and leg size for a 45° equal-leg fillet weld.**

**Model Answer:**

The **effective throat thickness (t_e)** is the perpendicular distance from the weld root to the weld face — it is the minimum cross-sectional dimension of the weld and represents the plane along which the weld is assumed to fail in shear.

For a 45° equal-leg fillet weld:

$$
t_e = 0.707 \cdot s
$$

**Derivation:**

The fillet weld cross-section is an isosceles right triangle with legs s and hypotenuse s√2. The throat (altitude to the hypotenuse) is:

$$
t_e = \frac{\text{Area of triangle} \times 2}{\text{Hypotenuse}} = \frac{(s^2/2) \times 2}{s\sqrt{2}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{2}} = 0.707 \, s
$$

---

## Part B: 14-Mark Questions (ESE Module Internal Choice Pattern)

### Question A (14 Marks)

**[KTU University Exam - Model Paper 2024 Scheme]**

**(a) A bracket carrying a vertical load of 120 kN is welded to a column flange using two vertical fillet welds of length 180 mm each, spaced 250 mm apart. The load is applied at an eccentricity of 300 mm from the face of the column. Determine the required leg size of the fillet weld if the allowable shear stress is 110 N/mm². (7 marks)**

**Step-by-Step Model Solution:**

**Step 1 — Data Given**

P = 120,000 N; L = 2 × 180 = 360 mm; spacing = 250 mm → c = 125 mm;  
e = 300 mm; τ_allow = 110 N/mm²; s = ?

**Step 2 — Direct Shear Stress**

$$
\tau_{d} = \frac{P}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot L} = \frac{120{,}000}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot 360} = \frac{471.3}{s} \text{ N/mm}^2
$$

**Step 3 — Moment of Inertia of Weld Group**

$$
I = 2 \cdot L_i \cdot c^{2} = 2 \cdot 180 \cdot (125)^{2} = 5{,}625{,}000 \text{ mm}^3\text{-equivalent}
$$

**Step 4 — Bending Moment**

$$
M = P \cdot e = 120{,}000 \cdot 300 = 36 \times 10^{6} \text{ N·mm}
$$

**Step 5 — Bending Shear Stress at Extreme Weld**

$$
\tau_{b} = \frac{M \cdot c}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot I} = \frac{36 \times 10^{6} \cdot 125}{0.707 \cdot s \cdot 5{,}625{,}000} = \frac{1131.6}{s} \text{ N/mm}^2
$$

**Step 6 — Total Maximum Shear Stress**

$$
\tau_{max} = \tau_{d} + \tau_{b} = \frac{471.3}{s} + \frac{1131.6}{s} = \frac{1602.9}{s} \text{ N/mm}^2
$$

**Step 7 — Solve for s**

$$
s = \frac{1602.9}{110} = 14.57 \text{ mm}
$$

**Step 8 — Adopt Standard Size**

Provide s = **16 mm** (next higher standard size).

$$
\boxed{\,s_{adopted} = 16 \text{ mm}\,}
$$

**Step 9 — Check Minimum Length Criterion**

4s = 4 × 16 = 64 mm < 180 mm ✓ (satisfactory)

---

**(b) Explain the various types of welded joints with neat sketches. State the advantages and limitations of welded joints. (7 marks)**

**Model Answer:**

**Types of Welded Joints (with Applications):**

1. **Butt Joint** — Plates in the same plane joined at edges. Used in pressure vessels, pipelines, and plate girders. Edge preparation (V, U, J) is required for thickness > 6 mm.

2. **Lap Joint** — One plate overlaps another. Used in sheet metal work, bracing members. Simple and economical; subject to eccentric loading.

3. **Tee Joint** — Two plates meet at 90° forming a T-shape. Used in beam-column connections, stiffener attachment. Single or double fillet welds on both sides.

4. **Corner Joint** — Two plates meet at a right angle along their edges. Used in box sections, frames, tanks.

5. **Edge Joint** — Plates placed edge-to-edge with welds on the edges. Used in light-gauge sheet metal flooring.

**Advantages of Welded Joints:**
- High strength-to-weight ratio
- Permanent, leak-proof joints
- Flexibility in design (any shape/size)
- Smooth profile, no protrusions
- Economical for mass production
- Continuous load transfer, no stress concentrations at bolt holes
- Can join dissimilar metals (with compatible filler)

**Limitations of Welded Joints:**
- Requires skilled labor and quality control
- Heat-affected zone (HAZ) may cause metallurgical changes
- Residual stresses and distortion
- Difficult to inspect (NDT required)
- Brittle failure possible at low temperatures
- Difficult to dismantle for repair

---

### Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice

**[KTU University Exam - Model Paper 2024 Scheme]**

**(a) A C-shaped fillet weld is used to attach a bracket to a column. The weld consists of three sides of a rectangle: two vertical welds of 150 mm length each at the sides, and one horizontal weld of 200 mm length at the bottom. The bracket carries a vertical load of 60 kN at a horizontal eccentricity of 100 mm from the centroid of the weld group. Calculate the maximum shear stress in the weld if the leg size is 8 mm. (7 marks)**

**Step-by-Step Model Solution:**

**Step 1 — Weld Geometry and Centroid**

Taking the bottom-left corner as origin, the three weld segments are:
- Bottom horizontal: y = 0, length 200 mm
- Left vertical: y from 0 to 150 mm, length 150 mm
- Right vertical: y from 0 to 150 mm, length 150 mm

Because of symmetry, the centroid lies on the y-axis at:
$$
\bar{y} = \frac{200 \cdot 0 + 150 \cdot 75 + 150 \cdot 75}{200 + 150 + 150} = \frac{22{,}500}{500} = 45 \text{ mm}
$$

**Step 2 — Total Weld Length and Polar Moment of Inertia**

L_total = 200 + 150 + 150 = **500 mm**

Compute I_x (about centroidal axis):

For the bottom weld (distance = 45 mm from centroid):
$$
I_{x1} = L_1 \cdot d_1^2 = 200 \cdot (45)^2 = 405{,}000 \text{ mm}^3
$$

For each vertical weld (use parallel axis theorem, with d = 30 mm from centroid to its own centroid):
$$
I_{x2} = L_2 \cdot \bar{d}^2 + \frac{L_2^3}{12} = 150 \cdot (30)^2 + \frac{150^3}{12} = 135{,}000 + 281{,}250 = 416{,}250 \text{ mm}^3
$$

For both verticals: I_x2_total = 2 × 416,250 = 832,500 mm³

$$
I_x = 405{,}000 + 832{,}500 = 1{,}237{,}500 \text{ mm}^3
$$

For I_y, all welds lie at the same x-coordinate (zero, by symmetry):
$$
I_y = 0
$$

So I_p = I_x = 1,237,500 mm³

**Step 3 — Torsional Moment**

$$
T = P \cdot e = 60{,}000 \cdot 100 = 6 \times 10^{6} \text{ N·mm}
$$

**Step 4 — Direct Vertical Shear per Unit Length**

$$
q_{v} = \frac{P}{L_{total}} = \frac{60{,}000}{500} = 120 \text{ N/mm}
$$

**Step 5 — Identify Critical Point**

The critical point is the top corner of either vertical weld. At this point:
- r = distance from centroid = √(45² + 0²) ≈ vertical offset of top of weld
  - Top of left/right vertical weld is at y = 150 mm; distance from centroid = 150 − 45 = 105 mm
- Both direct shear (downward) and torsional shear (perpendicular to radius) act at this point.

**Step 6 — Torsional Shear at Critical Point**

$$
q_{T} = \frac{T \cdot r}{I_p} = \frac{6 \times 10^{6} \cdot 105}{1{,}237{,}500} = 509.1 \text{ N/mm}
$$

**Step 7 — Resultant Shear Force per Unit Length**

At the top of the vertical weld, q_v acts vertically downward and q_T acts horizontally (perpendicular to radius, which is vertical, so q_T is horizontal).

$$
q_{R} = \sqrt{q_{v}^{2} + q_{T}^{2}} = \sqrt{120^2 + 509.1^2} = \sqrt{14{,}400 + 259{,}183} = \sqrt{273{,}583} \approx 523.1 \text{ N/mm}
$$

**Step 8 — Throat Shear Stress**

$$
\tau = \frac{q_R}{0.707 \cdot s} = \frac{523.1}{0.707 \cdot 8} = \frac{523.1}{5.656} = 92.5 \text{ N/mm}^2
$$

$$
\boxed{\,\tau_{max} = 92.5 \text{ N/mm}^2\,}
$$

**Step 9 — Verification**

Compare with allowable (say 110 N/mm²): 92.5 < 110 ✓ **Safe design**.

---

**(b) Discuss the design considerations for welds subjected to dynamic and fatigue loading. Mention the IS 800:2007 recommendations for fatigue design of welded joints. (7 marks)**

**Model Answer:**

**Design Considerations for Dynamic / Fatigue Loading:**

1. **Stress Concentration:** Welds have inherent stress concentrations at the toe (weld-to-parent metal interface). Grinding the weld toe smooth (butt welds) can improve fatigue life by 50–100%.

2. **Weld Profile:** Convex welds have higher stress concentration than flat or concave welds. As per IS 800:2007, convexity should be limited.

3. **Weld Defects:** Undercuts, porosity, slag inclusions, lack of fusion, and lack of penetration act as crack initiation sites. All defects must be minimized and inspected by NDT (UT, RT, MPI).

4. **Residual Stresses:** Welding induces tensile residual stresses at the weld toe, which accelerate fatigue crack initiation. Post-weld heat treatment (PWHT) or peening can mitigate this.

5. **Residual Stresses + Tension:** The combination of tensile residual stress and applied tensile stress means the effective mean stress is high, reducing fatigue life.

6. **Weld Type and Orientation:** Transverse welds have lower fatigue strength than longitudinal welds. Butt welds with full penetration and ground flush have the best fatigue performance.

**IS 800:2007 Recommendations:**
- Fatigue design uses **stress range** (not peak stress) as per Clause 13.
- Fatigue strength classification into classes (F-class: F1, F2, F3, F4) based on detail type.
- S-N curves (Wöhler curves) provided for each class.
- Partial safety factor γ_mf = 1.0 for fatigue (since stress range controls).
- High-cycle (≥ 10⁵ cycles) and low-cycle regimes considered separately.
- For welded connections, the **fatigue stress range** must be ≤ **f_ft** at the relevant number of cycles.

---

## KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mark-Loss Pitfalls in Weld Design Problems (KTU Board Papers):**
> 1. **Forgetting the 0.707 factor** — students often use s × L (leg area) instead of 0.707 × s × L (throat area). This **overestimates capacity** by 41% — design is unsafe, full marks lost.
> 2. **Not using parallel axis theorem** — for weld groups with eccentric loading, simply dividing moment by total length gives a wrong answer. Always compute I = Σ L_i × d_i².
> 3. **Mixing parallel and transverse welds** — for combined loading with both directions, use vector sum (Pythagoras), not algebraic sum.
> 4. **Ignoring minimum weld length rule (4s)** — if computed length is < 4s, the size governs and design is invalid.
> 5. **Not adopting standard leg size** — always round UP to next standard size: 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 22, 25 mm.
> 6. **Missing units** — N vs kN, mm vs cm, N/mm² vs MPa (same, but write it clearly).
> 7. **Not specifying code reference** — IS 800:2007 / IS 816:1969 / AWS D1.1 must be cited for any allowable stress.
> 8. **Drawing without labeling throat, leg, root** — sketches without labels lose **2 marks** in 14-mark problems.

---

## Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid-Revision Checklist for Weld Joint Design (Module 2)**

- **Five Joint Types:** Butt, Lap, Tee, Corner, Edge — know geometry and typical weld type for each.
- **Weld Types:** Fillet (triangular, throat = 0.707s), Groove (square, V, U, J), Plug/Slot, Spot/Seam.
- **Throat Thickness Formula:** t = 0.707 × s (45° equal leg) — memorize.
- **Throat Area:** A = 0.707 × s × L — basis of all strength calculations.
- **Failure Plane:** Always the throat (smallest area, max shear).
- **Direct Shear Stress:** τ = P / (0.707 × s × L).
- **Combined Loading:** Use Pythagorean sum √(τ_perp² + τ_parallel²).
- **Eccentric Loading (Bending + Direct):** Use I = Σ L_i d_i² (parallel axis theorem) and τ_max = M·c / (0.707·s·I) ± P / (0.707·s·L).
- **Torsion:** I_p = I_x + I_y; τ = T·r / (0.707·s·I_p).
- **Minimum Effective Length:** ≥ 4 × leg size (else size governs).
- **Maximum Effective Length in Lap:** ≤ 40 × throat thickness.
- **End Returns:** For end-loaded fillet welds, return length ≥ 2s.
- **Standard Leg Sizes (mm):** 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 18, 20, 22, 25.
- **Allowable Shear Stress (IS 800:2007):** ≈ 110–150 N/mm² (shop) and 100–130 N/mm² (field) depending on electrode and plate grade.
- **Transverse vs Parallel:** Transverse fillet weld is ~30% stronger (full throat + normal stress component) — IS 800 simplifies this.
- **AWS Symbols:** Arrow line + reference line + fillet triangle + leg size + length + pitch (for intermittent welds).
- **Fatigue Concerns:** Weld toe is the crack initiation site; grind smooth, use full-penetration butt welds where possible.
- **NDT for Welds:** Visual, DPT, MPI, UT, RT — required for critical joints (pressure vessels, bridges).
- **Common Industrial Applications:** Structural steel buildings, pressure vessels, bridges, ship hulls, automotive chassis, pipelines, aerospace.
- **Code References to Quote:** IS 800:2007, IS 816:1969, AWS D1.1, ASME Sec. VIII, API 1104.
- **Design Philosophy:** Strength + Economy + Serviceability + Manufacturability + Inspectability.
- **Dimensional Discipline:** Always work in N, mm, N/mm² (MPa). Show substitutions explicitly.
- **Free-Body Diagrams:** Always draw the FBD showing the weld as a line, with forces, moment, and centroid marked.
- **Vector Diagram for Torsion:** Show q_direct, q_torsion, and q_resultant as vectors at the critical point.
- **Final Adopted Size:** Always round UP to the next standard leg size.
- **Verify with Code Checks:** After sizing, verify minimum length, end returns, and parent metal capacity.
